newsitem.title: USA: "Liberal" becomes a dirty word in U.S. election.
newsitem.headline: "Liberal" becomes a dirty word in U.S. election.

text.p: For people in Europe and Latin America, where liberalism still means free market capitalism, Republican Bob Dole is the real liberal in this presidential election.

But the word "liberal" had a different evolution in North America, and Dole is using it to attack President Bill Clinton for everything from his ill-fated health care reform plan to the tax rise he pushed through Congress in 1993.

"It really boils down to a contest between the warmed-over liberal ideas of President Clinton and my common-sense conservative ideas that put the opportunities, safety and future of our children and families before government," Dole said in a nationwide radio address on Saturday.

Dole also has a new ad, "How to speak liberal," which contrasts Clinton's words with his actions, running this weekend on CNN and on local stations in Washington and Hartford, Connecticut, where the two candidates square off in the first presidential debate on Sunday.
The "L-word," as former President George Bush put it during the 1988 election, has become the most common insult hurled at Democratic candidates by conservative opponents.

Most Democrats -- with notable exceptions like Sen. Edward Kennedy of Massachusetts and former New York Gov. Mario Cuomo -- are dodging the barrage. Clinton even felt compelled last month to deny he was "a closet liberal."
But liberal has not always been a dirty word -- and until about 50 years ago, it meant the opposite of what it does now.

Ancient Roman writers used liberal to mean generous, and in the late 19th century British philosopher John Stuart Mill equated the term with a movement aimed at expanding the free market and reducing government restrictions.

On this side of the Atlantic, advocates of moderate government regulations began using the term "liberal" between 1900 and the First World War. President Woodrow Wilson used it to describe the peace programme he proposed after the war ended.
It was not until the 1930s, when President Franklin D. Roosevelt was looking for a term to describe his "New Deal," that "liberal" became synonymous with activist government.
At that point, the term still did not have a negative ring and Roosevelt's opponents preferred to call him a "socialist."
In fact, Roosevelt's predecessor Herbert Hoover complained about the theft of a Republican term.

By the late 1970s, former Vice President Spiro Agnew used the term "radical liberal" to attack Democrats who opposed the Vietnam War. At that point, liberal came to mean advocates of the welfare state, abortion rights and a loosening of the so-called family values of the 1950s, says George Washington University history professor Leo Ribuffo.
"You don't get out-and-out attacks on liberals per se, without the radical adjective, until the Reagan and Bush administrations," Ribuffo told Reuters.

These days, he said, many Democrats preferred the term "progressive" to describe their politics. They were reluctant to embrace the term once hailed proudly by the likes of John F. Kennedy, but now "tainted with these images of big spending, sexual depravity and marijuana smoke."
William Adams, a public policy expert at George Washington University, says the problem is that "liberalism has come to be associated with the excesses of its good intentions."
Many Americans, he argues, associate liberalism more with a coercive quota system than the historic civil rights breakthroughs of equal opportunity.

Some Americans, activists in the tiny Libertarian Party dedicated to downsizing government, are trying to reclaim the historic meaning of the term, but most political observers doubt "liberal" will shed its negative image anytime soon.
"This is one rhetorical battle that the conservatives seem to have won," Adams said.

Dole's campaign seems to be getting through to voters, with the latest New York Times/CBS News poll showing that 43 percent perceived Clinton as a liberal, up from 38 percent who described him that way before the 1992 election.
